mars.name: Mars
mars.water: Confirmed as water ice at the poles and in shallow subsurface deposits; strong geological evidence of ancient rivers, lakes, and possibly an ocean billions of years ago.
mars.organic_molecules: Organic (carbon-based) molecules have been detected in Martian rocks by the Curiosity rover — a building block for life, not evidence of it.
mars.energy_sources: Potential chemical energy sources exist in subsurface minerals; sunlight is abundant at the surface but the atmosphere offers little protection from radiation.
mars.radiation: High. Mars lacks a global magnetic field and has a very thin atmosphere, so surface radiation levels are far higher than Earth's.
mars.temperature: Average around -63°C; well below the freezing point of water at the surface today.
mars.atmosphere: Thin, over 95% carbon dioxide, with surface pressure less than 1% of Earth's.
mars.known_evidence: Ancient riverbeds, mineral deposits that only form in liquid water, seasonal methane fluctuations of debated origin.
mars.unknowns: Whether ancient Mars ever supported life, and whether any microbial life could persist in protected subsurface niches today.
mars.know: Mars had liquid water and a thicker atmosphere billions of years ago.
mars.suspect: Subsurface environments today might shield liquid water and organic chemistry from surface radiation.
mars.unknown: Whether life ever existed on Mars, in the past or present — no evidence of life has been found.

europa.name: Europa
europa.water: Strong evidence of a deep, salty liquid water ocean beneath its icy shell — potentially more water than all of Earth's oceans combined.
europa.organic_molecules: Not yet directly confirmed on the surface, though the chemistry needed to produce them is considered plausible.
europa.energy_sources: Tidal heating from Jupiter's gravity keeps the subsurface ocean liquid; possible chemical energy from interaction between the ocean and rocky seafloor.
europa.radiation: Very high at the icy surface due to Jupiter's intense radiation belts — but this radiation does not reach the subsurface ocean.
europa.temperature: Surface averages around -160°C; the subsurface ocean is insulated and far warmer.
europa.known_evidence: Surface fractures and 'chaos terrain' consistent with an active ocean below; a possible induced magnetic field suggesting a conductive (salty) ocean.
europa.unknowns: Direct composition of the ocean, whether hydrothermal activity exists on the seafloor, and whether any biosignatures are present.
europa.know: Europa almost certainly has a global subsurface liquid water ocean.
europa.suspect: Tidal heating could drive hydrothermal activity similar to environments on Earth where life thrives without sunlight.
europa.unknown: Whether the ocean has ever hosted any biological activity — this remains a leading open question in astrobiology.

enceladus.name: Enceladus
enceladus.water: Confirmed subsurface liquid water ocean, directly sampled via geysers erupting from the south pole.
enceladus.organic_molecules: Simple organic molecules and complex carbon-based compounds have been directly detected in the geyser plumes by the Cassini spacecraft.
enceladus.energy_sources: Tidal heating from Saturn; direct evidence of hydrothermal activity on the ocean floor has been found in the form of silica nanograins, which typically require hot water reacting with rock.
enceladus.radiation: Low at the surface compared to Europa, and irrelevant to the shielded subsurface ocean.
enceladus.temperature: Surface averages around -198°C; the ocean itself is kept liquid by tidal heating.
enceladus.atmosphere: No global atmosphere, but active water-vapor plumes at the south pole.
enceladus.known_evidence: Direct sampling of plume material found water, simple organics, and molecular hydrogen — a potential energy source for microbial metabolism, if life existed.
enceladus.unknowns: Whether the chemical conditions found so far are actually being used by any biological process, or simply reflect non-biological geochemistry.
enceladus.know: Enceladus has an active subsurface ocean with hydrothermal chemistry.
enceladus.suspect: The detected hydrogen could, in principle, support microbial metabolism similar to some Earth deep-sea vent organisms.
enceladus.unknown: Whether any microbial life is actually present — no biosignature has been confirmed.

titan.name: Titan
titan.water: No liquid water on the surface (too cold), but a subsurface liquid water ocean is suspected beneath the icy crust.
titan.organic_molecules: Abundant. Titan's thick atmosphere is rich in complex organic chemistry, and its surface features lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.
titan.energy_sources: Weak sunlight reaches the surface through the hazy atmosphere; internal tidal heating may support a subsurface ocean.
titan.radiation: Low at the surface — Titan's thick atmosphere and distance from the Sun shield it well.
titan.temperature: Surface averages around -179°C, far too cold for liquid water but suitable for liquid methane and ethane.
titan.atmosphere: Thick, nitrogen-rich atmosphere denser than Earth's, with a complete methane-based weather cycle.
titan.known_evidence: Cassini-Huygens directly imaged lakes, rivers, and rain of liquid hydrocarbons — the only other place in the Solar System with stable surface liquids.
titan.unknowns: Whether 'exotic' life based on liquid methane rather than water could theoretically exist — a genuinely speculative idea explored by astrobiologists.
titan.know: Titan has a complete liquid cycle on its surface, just using methane instead of water.
titan.suspect: Its rich organic chemistry makes it a valuable natural laboratory for studying the chemical steps that might precede life.
titan.unknown: Whether any form of chemistry there could be considered 'alive' by any definition — highly speculative and unconfirmed.
